title: Abu Bakr's first speech
hookLine: obey me as long as I obey Allah, and if I go wrong, set me right (sirah)

lines: A MAN ASKING TO BE WATCHED.
cards: A new leader stands up in front of the people for the first time. What does a person usually say in that moment? Something about strength, a plan, how things are going to be better now.
Abu Bakr, the Prophet's longtime friend, has just received the pledge of the community in Medina.
Sunni Muslims remember this as the moment he took office as caliph; Shia Muslims, as this week has shown, remember the succession differently.
Either way, the speech the sources give him is short, and it doesn't sound like a victory speech at all. It sounds like a man asking to be watched. Today: Abu Bakr's first speech.

teach.h: I AM NOT THE BEST OF YOU.
teach.b: The speech comes to us through the sirah, the early biographies of the Prophet, in the work of Ibn Ishaq as passed on by Ibn Hisham. In paraphrase, it goes like this.
I have been put in charge of you, and I am not the best of you. If I do well, help me.

teach.h: IF I DO WRONG, SET ME RIGHT.
teach.b: If I do wrong, set me right. Truthfulness is a trust, and lying is a betrayal.

teach.h: THE WEAK ARE STRONG WITH ME.
teach.b: The weak among you is strong in my eyes until I get him his right, and the strong among you is weak in my eyes until I take from him what he owes.

teach.h: NO OBEDIENCE IF I DISOBEY GOD.
teach.b: Obey me as long as I obey God and His Messenger, and if I disobey them, you owe me no obedience. Take it a line at a time. I am not the best of you: he opens by lowering himself, not raising himself.
Set me right: he hands the people the job of correcting him. The weak and the strong: power usually leans toward the strong, and he says it will lean the other way until rights are paid.
And the limit: obedience stops where he stops obeying God. A leader who writes his own limit into his first words is telling the people where the line is before anyone has to find it.
In Sunni teaching, this speech is read as a picture of how authority should sit on a person: lightly, and under God.

how: Abu Bakr's first address is often quoted by Sunni Muslims in sermons and teaching about leadership, especially its lines asking the people to help him when he does well and set him right when he does wrong.

games.q: you've just been chosen to lead a grieving community. it's your first time speaking to them as leader. what do you say?
o: promise them you'll make everything better.
tell them you're not the best of them, and ask them to correct you.
remind them they must obey you.
games.why: the sirah gives Abu Bakr the second: I am not the best of you; if I do well, help me; if I do wrong, set me right.

practice: Think of one place where you hold a little authority: at work, at home, over a younger sibling, in a group chat you run.
Ask yourself honestly who would tell you if you were getting it wrong, and hold that question until it stops feeling dangerous.

wordCard.voice: Abu Bakr. The Prophet's longtime friend, who in his first speech as leader said: I am not the best of you; if I do well, help me; if I do wrong, set me right. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'set me right', the request at the heart of the speech.

carryVoice: Your line: set me right. And the week: the generation, the saqifah, two tellings, Ghadir Khumm, Fatimah, and a leader asking to be corrected. That's the week.

sources.ref: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, from Ibn Ishaq (Abu Bakr's address after the pledge)
